routes.description: Establish early individual and group appearance testimony, interpret it as bodily resurrection testimony, and compare resurrection with naturalistic alternatives under historical explanatory criteria.
routes.successCriteria: The reported death, appearances, conversions, bodily-resurrection belief, and resulting movement must be sufficiently supported and collectively better expected under resurrection than under the proposed natural explanations.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus rose and that resurrection explains the early Christian testimony more adequately than the available naturalistic alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Establish that early, apostolically connected sources report appearances to individuals and groups.
Establish that the relevant testimony concerns Jesus's transformed physical body rather than visions alone.
Show that hallucination, contagion, legendary development, and related natural mechanisms do not adequately explain the reported evidence.
Apply explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and avoidance of unsupported assumptions to the competing hypotheses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Integrate Jesus's prior claims, reported deeds, prediction, appearances, conversions, and the resulting movement into the comparison.
Preserve the historical usefulness of the Gospel core despite literary shaping and peripheral differences.

routes.description: Require evidence proportionate to resurrection's low background probability and explain the testimony through established psychological, social, and literary processes.
routes.successCriteria: The surviving testimony must remain insufficiently exceptional to overcome resurrection's prior burden while visions, social contagion, missing-body scenarios, and tradition development remain adequate natural possibilities.

motionBridge.description: Show that the early Christian testimony does not warrant resurrection over established natural classes of explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that an unprecedented divine resurrection requires exceptionally strong confirming evidence.
Explain individual and group appearance beliefs through culturally conditioned visions, suggestion, and charismatic contagion.
Show that the early epistolary evidence lacks the detail needed to establish shared encounters with a physical Jesus or verification of an empty grave.
Account for detailed resurrection narratives through legendary growth, redaction, literary imitation, and mythmaking.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain that loss, removal, or nonverification of a body can accompany appearance beliefs without resurrection.
Compare the reported narrow appearance pattern with what a local visionary movement and a universally revealing deity would predict.

sections.title: Historical Method and Prior Probability
sections.rationale: The governing comparison depends on whether explanatory criteria can bracket resurrection's prior probability or whether its lack of established precedent imposes an exceptional evidential burden.

sections.title: Early Testimony and Bodily Resurrection
sections.rationale: The motion turns centrally on whether the earliest evidence reports apostolically connected encounters with a transformed physical Jesus or sparse and culturally conditioned visionary experiences.

sections.title: Psychological and Group-Appearance Mechanisms
sections.rationale: A principal clash concerns whether known psychological and social processes can generate the reported individual and group experiences and the ensuing bodily-resurrection belief.

sections.title: Cumulative Explanatory Comparison
sections.rationale: The central inference requires comparing how the resurrection and naturalistic routes account for the combined reports rather than treating each appearance, conversion, or missing-body claim in isolation.

sections.title: Gospel Literary and Historical Value
sections.rationale: The detailed bodily and empty-tomb narratives depend partly on whether Gospel composition and disagreement preserve a usable historical core or instead indicate literary and legendary development.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Historical hypotheses should be compared by explanatory scope, explanatory power, avoidance of unsupported assumptions, and plausibility against accepted facts.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs continuously within Licona's formally introduced affirmative opening statement.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the affirmative's stated criteria for comparing historical hypotheses and therefore requires no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly supplies the methodological framework later used for the central comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is strong central-tier contact because it supplies the governing historical-comparison method, though it does not itself complete the motion.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Paul's resurrection teaching concerns Jesus's transformed physical corpse, and resurrection is offered as the explanation of the reported individual and group appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Licona's affirmative opening and continues his Pauline evidential argument.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Paul's letters depict vision-prone Christian communities and do not establish that the appearances were detailed, shared encounters with a physically risen Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person skeptical analysis remains within Carrier's formally allocated opening statement.

components.text: Whether Paul's appearance language establishes encounters with a transformed physical corpse rather than revelation or vision.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant contrary material within the nonanswer class because it challenges a psychological profile without resolving the earlier source-based demand.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Cognitive dissonance is a testable explanatory hypothesis rather than a clinical diagnosis and is inherently likelier than a divine apparition absent strong contrary evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly clarifies the challenged hypothesis and defends the naturalistic comparison characteristic of Carrier's stated position.

components.text: Whether a natural psychological explanation must establish that the apostles possessed a clinical schizotypal profile.

response.rationale: Carrier justifies replacing the clinical-profile demand with comparative assessment of a testable cognitive-dissonance mechanism, preserving the legitimate question of whether a natural psychological process is likelier than apparition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe explicitly explains why diagnosis is unnecessary and answers the preserved comparative-mechanism question.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hypothesis is clearly separated from diagnosis and expressly limited to an inherently likelier explanation absent strong contrary evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is qualified, but inherent superiority is asserted without supplying a base rate or case-specific likelihood in this span.

charity.alternative: The apostles' behavior may conflict with a specific pathological profile offered for hallucination.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cognitive dissonance does not require that clinical profile and remains a distinct hypothesis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Distinguishing a testable explanatory hypothesis from clinical diagnosis validly answers the profile objection, though comparative probability needs further premises.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally attacks the affirmative claim that natural psychological alternatives are inadequate, while remaining narrower than a complete mechanism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response accurately isolates the narrower force of the objection and preserves it while defending a different psychological mechanism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly presents cognitive dissonance as a more likely natural hypothesis than divine apparition, subject to contrary evidence, rather than as a diagnosis.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Jesus's religious claims, reputed miracles, resurrection prediction, and reported appearances to friends, foes, individuals, and groups create a cumulative context stronger than a merely missing body.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained turn advances Licona's cumulative resurrection case and explicitly contrasts Jesus with the preceding David Koresh example.

components.text: Whether cognitive dissonance is inherently likelier than divine apparition absent unusually strong contrary evidence.
Whether resurrection's lack of precedent requires evidence stronger than the testimony presented.
Whether the early letters establish physical shared encounters rather than visions.

response.rationale: The cumulative context supplies potentially relevant contrary evidence, but it assumes rather than demonstrates the inadequacy of natural mechanisms and does not directly answer the comparative-prior or sparse-source demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant nonanswer because the cumulative facts bear on comparison but do not contact the decisive inferential premises of the selected objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative contrast is clear, but reported miracles, predictions, and appearances are grouped without consistently separating reports from established facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker conditionally acknowledges that natural explanations must first be shown inadequate, but the excerpt then leans on that unsettled condition.

charity.alternative: A missing body can combine with psychologically and culturally generated appearance beliefs.
charity.decisiveQualification: A cumulative list favors resurrection only if its components are independently supported and more expected under that hypothesis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A cumulative context can distinguish the case from a bare missing body, but the inference depends on the asserted inadequacy of alternatives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several relevant reported features are enumerated, yet their historical status, independence, and comparative likelihoods are not defended here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary cumulative-context bridge but does not directly complete a central or motion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the need to address natural explanations but gives their conjunctive alternative only limited treatment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt combines Jesus's claimed miracles, prediction, and reported appearances to friends, foes, individuals, and groups, contrasting them with a merely missing body.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Combining rare missing-body and appearance reports does not favor resurrection because their natural causes remain jointly more probable than supernatural causes.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn answers Licona's cumulative case with Carrier's characteristic comparative-probability analysis of natural and supernatural conjunctions.

components.text: Whether combining a missing body with diverse appearance reports makes resurrection comparatively superior to natural alternatives.

response.rationale: The move directly answers the cumulative inference by comparing the conjunction of natural causes with the conjunction of supernatural causes and denying that combined rarity favors resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative inference explicitly, although the numerical assumptions remain illustrative rather than established.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conjunction comparison is recoverable and consistent, but its probability assignments and independence assumptions remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The direction of comparison is stated firmly despite hypothetical and undeveloped component probabilities, though the speaker flags illustrative uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Multiple mutually reinforcing facts may be collectively more expected if resurrection occurred.
charity.decisiveQualification: Their conjunction helps only after comparing the joint likelihoods under both natural and supernatural hypotheses.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative-conjunction point is valid in form, but the result depends on component probabilities and dependence relations not supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a useful probabilistic structure, yet its illustrative rates and the resulting ordering lack empirical or formal support in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the affirmative motion bridge by denying that the combined evidence favors resurrection over natural causes.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move directly addresses the strongest cumulative form rather than treating each reported fact in isolation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier expressly compares the rarity of missing bodies and divine appearances and argues that their natural conjunction remains more probable than the supernatural conjunction.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The appearance sequence can be explained through a private vision followed by charismatic suggestion and progressively larger ecstatic group experiences.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier is asked what happened in group appearances and develops a sustained first-person naturalistic reconstruction using comparative cult behavior.

components.text: Whether reported individual and group appearances require encounters with a transformed physical corpse.
Whether appearances to individuals and progressively larger groups resist natural explanation.
Whether a natural account requires a uniform schizotypal profile among the apostles.

charity.alternative: The reports may describe multiple genuine encounters with a bodily risen Jesus rather than socially generated experiences.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses individual and group appearances fairly, while compressing the evidential demand concerning their particular bodily content.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes a leader's private vision becoming socially contagious through charismatic anchoring, inspiration, guidance, and suggestion.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Reported ordinary-state features and the resulting belief in bodily resurrection with an empty grave make altered-state hallucinations an inadequate explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker cites research on ordinary versus altered consciousness and then advances Licona's recurring bodily-resurrection objection to hallucination theories.

components.text: Whether altered states, suggestion, and charismatic contagion can produce the reported bodily-resurrection belief.
Whether vision reports remain compatible with belief in a physically risen Jesus and an empty grave.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the mechanism's decisive content problem explicitly, though it does not answer every social step in the proposed sequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the vision-mechanism bridge by focusing on whether that mechanism predicts the reported belief's bodily content.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona

components.text: Whether the combined reported facts are more probable under natural causes than under resurrection.
Whether hallucination and contagion explain the individual and group appearance reports.
Whether the affirmative evidence is strong enough given resurrection's background burden.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a high partial answer because it reaches the decisive comparative component but leaves the prior-burden component substantially unanswered.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Sparse epistolary evidence is not exceptional enough to overcome resurrection's low prior probability, while culturally conditioned visions can explain the early Christian beliefs.

components.text: Whether resurrection explains the combined early testimony better than culturally conditioned visions and other ordinary causes.
Whether visions fail to explain bodily-resurrection and empty-grave belief.
Whether early apostolic appearance testimony is sufficiently detailed and exceptional.
Whether the epistles establish unnatural bodily encounters.

moves.proposition: Plausibility corresponds to prior probability, so a hypothesis invoking unestablished causes requires exceptionally strong evidence that the resurrection case lacks.

components.text: Whether plausibility can function as an ordinary criterion without incorporating resurrection's very low prior probability.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
